function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a complete, ready‑to‑use set of files that you can drop into the **nodejs‑welcome** repository, followed by a short “cheat‑sheet” of the Git commands you’ll need to run locally to commit and push the changes.

> **NOTE** – I can’t actually clone or push to your repo from here, but the files below are fully functional and ready for you to copy‑paste into the repo’s root (or the appropriate sub‑folders).

---

## 1. Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the root of the repo:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# Base image – Alpine is small and fast
FROM node:18-alpine

# Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /app

# Copy package.json & package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port your app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Default command – change if your entry point is different
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * Uses the official Node 18 Alpine image – small, secure, and up‑to‑date.  
> * Installs only production dependencies (`npm ci --only=production`) so the image stays lean.  
> * Exposes port 3000 (the common default for Express apps). Adjust if your app uses another port.

---

## 2. Kubernetes YAML

Create a file named `k8s.yaml` (or split into `deployment.yaml` & `service.yaml`) in the root of the repo:

```yaml
# k8s.yaml
# ------------------------------------
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your registry if needed
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port exposed inside the cluster
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Deploys 2 replicas of your app.  
> * Exposes the app via a `ClusterIP` service on port 80 (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).  
> * Uses the image that will be built/pushed by the GitHub Actions workflow (see below).

---

## 3. GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
# ------------------------------------
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Set up Node.js
      - name: Set up Node.js
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: '18'

      # Install dependencies
      - name: Install dependencies
        run: npm ci

      # Run tests (optional – remove if you don’t have tests)
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test

      # Build Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} .

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Push Docker image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Tag the image as `latest` and push
      - name: Tag & push latest
        run: |
          docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Key points**  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret for authentication to GHCR.  
> * Builds the image with the commit SHA as the tag, then pushes both the SHA‑tagged image and a `latest` tag.  
> * If you prefer Docker Hub or another registry, replace the `registry`, `username`, and `password` fields accordingly.

---

## 4. Git Commands (run locally)

```bash
# 1. Clone the repo (if you haven’t already)
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome

# 2. Add the new files
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 3. Commit
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"

# 4. Push to main
git push origin main
```

> **Tip** – If you’re working on a feature branch, replace `main` with your branch name and merge/pull‑request once the changes are reviewed.

---

## 5. Quick sanity check

After pushing, you should see:

1. **GitHub Actions** → “CI” job runs automatically on the `main` branch push.  
2. **GHCR** → The image `ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:<sha>` and `latest` tags appear.  
3. **Kubernetes** → If you apply `k8s.yaml` to a cluster, you’ll get a deployment with 2 pods and a service exposing port 80.

---

### Done!

Drop the files into the repo, run the Git commands above, and you’ll have a fully automated CI pipeline that builds, tests, and publishes a Docker image, plus ready‑to‑apply Kubernetes manifests. Happy coding!
